key_terms.meaning: Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter; the hardware block that shifts a byte out and in as a serial frame, with no shared clock line.
Signal symbols sent per second; for a UART it equals bits per second, and with 8-N-1 framing the byte rate is baud rate ÷ 10.
The single 0 bit that opens every UART frame and lets the receiver align its sampling clock to the falling edge.
Standard that fixes the voltage levels and connector for a serial link: logic 1 is sent as −3 V to −15 V and logic 0 as +3 V to +15 V.
Serial Peripheral Interface; a four-wire synchronous bus (SCLK, MOSI, MISO, CS) with one master and full-duplex transfer.
Active-low SPI line, one per slave, that tells a slave to listen; without it a slave ignores the clock.
Two-wire synchronous bus (SDA data, SCL clock) with 7-bit device addresses and an acknowledge bit after every byte.
In I2C the receiver pulls SDA low during the ninth clock so the transmitter knows the byte arrived.
Controller Area Network; a twisted-pair differential multi-master bus where any node may transmit, used in vehicles and machinery.
CAN logic 0 is dominant and logic 1 recessive; when two nodes transmit at once, any 0 on the bus overrides a 1, so the lower-ID frame wins.
Local Interconnect Network; a single 12 V wire master-slave sub-bus at up to 20 kbit/s for cheap switches and motors in a car.
An addressable buffer inside a USB device; transfers are described by endpoint number plus direction (IN or OUT).
Parallel instrument bus (also called GPIB) with 8 data lines plus handshake and control lines, used to link lab instruments to a controller.
Bluetooth Low Energy; short-range 2.4 GHz link built for small bursts of data and coin-cell power budgets.
Low-rate mesh network on IEEE 802.15.4 at 2.4 GHz, used for many small nodes that relay each other's messages.
Long-range wide-area network using chirp spread spectrum; a few bytes per message over kilometres at very low power.
The server in a publish/subscribe system that receives messages on topics and forwards them to every subscribed client.
Constrained Application Protocol; a request/response protocol carried over UDP, designed for small devices and lossy links.
Advanced High-performance Bus in AMBA; a pipelined on-chip bus with separate address and data phases and burst transfers.
Advanced Peripheral Bus in AMBA; a simple non-pipelined bus for slow, low-power peripherals such as timers and UARTs.

takeaways: A UART sends bytes asynchronously using a start bit, data bits, an optional parity bit and a stop bit; RS-232 only adds the voltage rules and connector for that bit stream.
SPI is fast and simple but needs one chip-select wire per slave, while I2C uses two wires in total and pays for it with lower speed and addressing overhead.
CAN lets several nodes share one differential pair because dominant bits override recessive bits, so collisions become arbitration, not data loss.
LIN is a cheap single-wire sub-bus under a CAN gateway; it does not compete with CAN, it extends it to low-cost switches and motors.
USB puts all bus control in the host, so a device never transmits unless the host polls it through an endpoint and a defined transfer type.
Parallel interfaces move a whole word per clock or handshake, which is fast but needs many wires and short distances.
Wireless choice is a trade between range, data rate, power and topology; no single radio wins on all four.

IoT systems are layered: perception layer sensors, network layer links, middleware layer brokers and storage, application layer services; MQTT and CoAP sit in the transport-and-above region that carries the data.
AMBA splits on-chip traffic into AHB for high-speed pipelined masters and APB for slow peripherals, with an arbiter granting the bus and a decoder selecting the slave.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for a labelled frame or timing diagram, a written comparison table across two or three buses, and a short justification of the bus chosen for a stated product, so practise drawing the diagrams quickly and naming each signal line.

bank.q: Explain the frame format of an asynchronous UART byte with 8-N-1 framing. Name each bit, give its purpose, and state the byte rate when the baud rate is 9600 bit/s.
outline: Idle line held high; falling edge of start bit begins the frame
One start bit (0), eight data bits least significant first, no parity, one stop bit (1)
Total 10 bit times per byte, so 9600 ÷ 10 = 960 bytes per second
Receiver samples near the middle of each bit; mismatch between the two clocks limits how many bits may be framed together
Optional parity bit gives single-bit error detection only

bank.q: Compare SPI and I2C on number of wires, speed, addressing, and multi-master capability. Draw the wire connections for one master with three slaves on each bus.
outline: SPI: 3 shared lines plus one chip select per slave; I2C: 2 lines total (SDA, SCL)
SPI typically tens of Mbit/s; I2C 100 kbit/s standard mode, 400 kbit/s fast mode
SPI selects by hardware chip-select line, no addressing; I2C uses a 7-bit address plus read/write bit
I2C has acknowledge bits and clock stretching, and supports multi-master with arbitration
Draw SPI slaves in parallel with separate CS lines; I2C slaves in parallel on the same two wires, each with pull-up resistors

bank.q: Explain why CAN uses a differential twisted pair and define dominant and recessive bits. Show how bit-wise arbitration decides which of two nodes continues transmitting.
outline: Two wires, CAN_H and CAN_L; the receiver reads the difference, so common-mode noise cancels
Logic 0 dominant, logic 1 recessive; wired-AND behaviour on the bus
Every node listens while it transmits and backs off on the first mismatch
Frame identifier decides priority: lower numeric identifier has more leading dominant bits and wins
Losing node becomes a receiver and retries later; no data is destroyed

bank.q: List the layers of an IoT architecture and state the job of each, giving one protocol or device type found at each layer.
outline: Perception layer: sensors and actuators, signal conditioning, device firmware
Network layer: links and gateways (Wi-Fi, BLE, LoRaWAN, cellular), addressing and routing
Middleware layer: broker, message store, device registry, data cleaning
Application layer: dashboards, analytics, user services
Name MQTT or CoAP for the messaging that crosses network and middleware

bank.q: A master must read four I2C temperature sensors on one board, but two of them are fixed at the same 7-bit address. Describe the problem and give two practical fixes, with the wiring change each needs.
outline: Address is set by the device, so two slaves answering the same address both drive SDA and the data is corrupted
Fix one: use an I2C multiplexer; master selects a channel before addressing the sensor
Fix two: put the duplicates on separate buses from separate master pins
Mention that many sensors have address-select pins that must be strapped differently at layout time
State the acknowledge behaviour that reveals a conflict

bank.q: Design a 500 kbit/s CAN network for a car with five nodes spread over about 20 m. Specify the wire, the termination, and describe step by step what happens when two nodes start sending at the same instant.
outline: Twisted pair, 120 Ω characteristic impedance, 120 Ω resistor at each physical end of the bus, not at every node
Stub lengths kept short; common ground reference
Both nodes send SOF, then compare identifier bits while listening
The node sending a recessive bit while the bus shows dominant loses and switches to receive
Winner finishes the frame; loser retries after the intermission; error counters and error frames protect the bus

bank.q: A UART link runs at 9600 bit/s with 8-N-1 framing between two boards clocked from different crystals. Calculate the byte rate, and explain what happens on the tenth bit if the receiver clock is 3 % fast.
outline: 10 bits per byte, so 960 bytes per second, about 1.04 ms per byte
Receiver samples at the middle of bit 0 and then every 10 bit times
3 % error accumulates across the frame, so the last sample drifts by roughly 3 % of 10 bits, about 0.3 bit time, still inside the bit
State the rule that total mismatch must stay well under half a bit time across the frame
Note that parity or a checksum catches the errors that do get through

bank.q: A housing society wants water-meter readings from 400 flats once every 30 minutes, on battery, with no per-flat internet connection. Choose a wireless technology and an application protocol, and justify both.
outline: Requirement: low data rate, long range through concrete, years of battery life, many nodes
LoRaWAN fits: kilometres of range, tiny payloads, class A duty cycling
Alternatively BLE or ZigBee with a per-block gateway if the block is small; state the trade
Use a concentrator gateway per block feeding the internet
CoAP or MQTT-SN over the constrained link, MQTT to the cloud broker
Say why Wi-Fi is rejected: power and access-point load

bank.q: Draw and explain a single AHB read burst of four beats. Label the address phase, the data phase, HREADY, and say where the arbiter and decoder act.
outline: Master drives HADDR and control in the address phase, then the slave's data comes back one cycle later in the data phase
Pipelining means the next address is issued while the previous data is still on the bus
Decoder uses HADDR to assert the correct HSELx; only that slave responds
Arbiter grants HGRANT to one master at a time and the granted master drives HTRANS
HREADY low inserts wait states in both phases; bursts of four beats keep the bus busy

bank.q: Compare USB and IEEE 488 as ways to connect instruments to a controller. Discuss topology, cable length, addressing, and why USB displaced the older bus in most labs.
outline: USB: tiered star through hubs, host-controlled polling, endpoints and four transfer types, up to a few metres per cable segment
IEEE 488: parallel party-line bus, 8 data lines plus handshake and control lines, up to 15 devices, short cable runs, slow by modern standards
Addressing: USB assigns addresses by enumeration; IEEE 488 uses dip-switch addresses on the bus
USB is cheap, hot-pluggable, powered from the bus and universal on PCs
IEEE 488 survives where a deterministic parallel handshake and mature instrument command sets matter

bank.q: A sensor node wakes every few minutes, sends a few hundred bytes, and sleeps. Compare MQTT over TCP with CoAP over UDP for this node. Recommend one and justify it in terms of power, reliability and the role of the broker.
outline: MQTT: long-lived TCP connection, keep-alive traffic, broker decouples publishers and subscribers, three quality-of-service levels
CoAP: UDP, short request/response, confirmable messages give retransmission without a standing connection, works with sleepy nodes
Power: MQTT keep-alives and TCP handshake cost energy; CoAP fits short bursts better
Reliability: TCP head-of-line blocking on a lossy radio link versus CoAP's own retransmission and optional observe
Recommend CoAP at the device with a gateway translating to MQTT for the cloud broker; or MQTT-SN

bank.q: An industrial product must link eight sensor boxes spread over 30 m in a plant with heavy motor noise. Evaluate RS-232, RS-485-style differential links, and CAN for this job, and justify one choice with bus, wiring and protocol details.
outline: RS-232 is single-ended, short range and referenced to a common ground; noise couples into the signal, so it is rejected
CAN is differential twisted pair, has built-in arbitration, error detection and retransmission, and is well supported by microcontrollers
State the distance-versus-bit-rate trade of a differential pair and the 120 Ω termination rule
Say what CAN gives that a plain differential link does not: framing, priorities, error confinement
Add that higher-layer choices (a CAN application profile or a simple master-slave protocol) follow from this decision

bank.q: Explain the roles of the arbiter and the decoder in AMBA. Argue why an SoC with an AHB segment and an APB segment needs a bridge between them, and what would go wrong without proper arbitration.
outline: Decoder: address-to-select, picks exactly one slave per transaction
Arbiter: grants the bus to one master, prevents two masters driving the shared address and data lines
Bridge holds AHB and APB timing apart, converts pipelined AHB to the simple APB setup and enable phases, and inserts wait states
Without arbitration two masters drive the bus and burn power or corrupt data
APB peripherals are slow, so the bridge's wait signalling is what keeps the fast side running correctly

glossary.def: The process that decides which of several devices may use a shared bus or medium at a given moment.
A link with no shared clock wire, where timing is recovered from the data itself.
Inserting an opposite bit after a run of identical bits so a receiver can keep its clock aligned, as CAN does after five equal bits.
A block that connects two different buses and translates their timing and signalling rules.
A server that receives published messages and forwards each one to the clients subscribed to its topic.
An I2C slave holding the clock line low to make the master wait until the slave is ready.
Sending a signal as the voltage difference between two wires so that noise common to both wires cancels out.
A complete, delimited unit of transmission that carries one or more data bytes plus control bits.
A link that can carry data in both directions at the same time, as SPI and UART do.
A device that joins two networks using different protocols and translates between them.
A pair of ready and accept signals that lets a sender and receiver agree when data is valid.
The device that starts and controls a transfer, and the device that answers it.
A network where nodes forward each other's messages, so a message can travel further than one radio hop.
A single extra bit that makes the number of 1s in a byte odd or even, catching some single-bit errors.
A messaging pattern where senders publish to a topic and receivers subscribe to topics, never addressing each other directly.
The CAN bit level that loses to the opposite level when two nodes transmit different values at the same time.
The trailing 1 bit of a UART frame that marks the end of the byte and allows a gap before the next start bit.
A resistor at the physical end of a bus that absorbs the signal energy and stops reflections.
The arrangement of the connections between nodes: bus, star, ring, mesh, or point to point.
A named string in a publish/subscribe system that decides which messages reach which subscribers.
Two insulated wires twisted together so that noise and crosstalk affect both wires almost equally.
An extra clock cycle inserted by a slow slave to delay the completion of a bus transfer.
